key_insight: Distal weight-bearing implants work best when biomechanical design, graded biomaterial interfaces, and coating durability are co-optimized to preserve load transfer while promoting long-term bone integration.
engineering_relevance: The paper shows that clinically viable transfemoral implants need gait-phase validated finite element models, fatigue-resistant Ti-HAp/FGM interfaces, and coating systems that can survive cyclic bending, shear, and micromotion.
method: Systematic review of DWBI geometry, biomaterials, and clinical translation literature
Trend analysis of 34 direct-contribution papers and 32 empirical studies
Synthesis of finite element analysis, graded Ti-HAp/FGM, and in-vivo osseointegration evidence
evidence_signal: The evidence base is still early-stage: more than half of the empirical studies were bench or simulation level, with fewer animal and human/clinical validations.
watch_item: A major implementation risk is overreliance on mechanistic analogs, since graded Ti-HAp/FGM evidence is largely not DWBI-specific and needs device-level fatigue and coating-integrity validation.
paper_title: Biomaterials and biomechanical design of distal weight-bearing implants: Computational modeling, biomaterial interfaces, and clinical translation
